title: When a spreadsheet stops being enough
author: Your Name
excerpt: Spreadsheets scale further than most developers admit — and then they fail suddenly. Here is how to tell which side of that line you are on.

content.text: Developers like to say a business has "outgrown" its spreadsheet long before it actually has. A well-built sheet is fast, flexible, free and understood by everyone in the office. Replacing one too early wastes money and usually makes the team slower.
The signals that actually matter
The moment to move is not a row count. It is when specific failures start repeating.

items: Two people edit the same rows and overwrite each other’s work.
A formula gets deleted and nobody notices for a week.
You cannot tell who changed a value, or when.
The same data is re-keyed into a second sheet.
People need different views but everyone sees everything.

content.text: Every one of those is a concurrency, integrity or permissions problem. Spreadsheets have no real answer to any of them, and no amount of colour coding fixes it.
The cheaper middle step

The jump people imagine is spreadsheet to full custom application. There is a step in between that solves most of these problems for a fraction of the cost: keep the sheet as the database and put a real interface on top of it.

With Google Apps Script, staff stop editing cells and start using forms. Entries get validated. Access is scoped by role. Every change is logged with a name and a timestamp. The accountant still opens the same sheet they always have.
When to actually build the application

Move to a real database when you need relationships across many record types, more than a handful of concurrent users, sub-second queries over large history, or an audit trail you could defend. Below that, a sheet with a proper interface will serve you well for years.

title: What to prepare before hiring a web developer
author: Your Name
excerpt: The projects that go smoothly are the ones where the client arrived with five specific things ready. None of them are technical.

content.text: Most delays on a web project are not caused by code. They are caused by waiting: for content, for a decision, for someone to say which of three logos is the real one. Arriving prepared can take weeks off a build.
1. Know what the site is for

Not "we need a website" — what should change once it exists. More enquiries? Fewer phone calls asking about prices? Orders taken without a marketplace commission? A clear objective settles a hundred smaller design decisions later.
2. Bring your content, or say you need help

Text about your services, real photographs, your logo in a usable format. Content is the single most common cause of a stalled project. If you do not have it, say so at the quotation stage so it can be planned rather than discovered.
3. Collect three sites you like
And, more usefully, say what you like about each one. "Clean" means nothing on its own; "I like how their pricing page answers everything before you contact them" is a brief.
4. Separate must-have from nice-to-have
A written feature list split into two columns keeps scope honest and gives you a lever if budget gets tight. Everything cannot be essential.
5. Decide who approves
One person with final say. Projects with three decision-makers and no tiebreaker take twice as long and usually end up designed by committee.

title: Google Apps Script: what it can and cannot do
author: Your Name
excerpt: An honest look at the limits — quotas, execution time, concurrency — and the kinds of systems that fit comfortably inside them.

content.text: Apps Script is genuinely underrated. It turns a spreadsheet into a multi-user system with a real interface, at a fraction of the cost of a custom application. It is also not a general-purpose application platform, and pretending otherwise leads to systems that fall over at exactly the wrong moment.
What it does well

items: Form-driven data entry with validation over an existing sheet.
Role-based access, so staff see only their own scope.
Scheduled jobs: daily summaries, reminders, report emails.
Document generation — invoices, payslips, certificates — as PDFs.
Integration across Sheets, Drive, Gmail and Calendar without extra infrastructure.

content.text: The real limits
Scripts have execution time limits and daily quotas. A poorly written loop that reads one row at a time will hit them quickly — batching reads and writes is not an optimisation, it is a requirement.

Concurrency is the harder constraint. Sheets do not offer row-level locking, so a system where many people write to the same rows simultaneously needs careful design, and past a certain volume needs a real database instead.
A reasonable rule of thumb

Up to roughly a dozen simultaneous users, tens of thousands of rows, and workflows measured in seconds rather than milliseconds, Apps Script is an excellent fit. Beyond that — heavy concurrent writes, large history, sub-second response — build on a proper database.
The good news is that migrating later is not wasted work: the data model you designed in Sheets is usually the same one you carry into MySQL.

title: Why your website is slow on mobile
author: Your Name
excerpt: It is almost always images, fonts and third-party scripts — in that order. A practical checklist you can run yourself.

content.text: A site that loads instantly on your laptop can take eight seconds on a mid-range phone on mobile data. Most visitors are on that phone, and a good share of them leave before the page appears.
Images: usually most of the problem

The most common single fault is a 4MB photograph straight from a camera, displayed 400 pixels wide. Serve appropriately sized images, use modern formats, and lazy-load anything below the fold. This alone often halves load time.
Fonts: the invisible delay

Every custom font weight is another download blocking text from appearing. Two weights of one family is usually plenty. Preconnect to the font host and use a swap strategy so text renders immediately in a fallback.
Third-party scripts: death by a thousand tags

Analytics, chat widgets, pixels, heatmaps, review embeds. Each one is a separate connection and often more JavaScript than your entire site. Audit them honestly and remove the ones nobody has looked at in six months.
How to check
Run PageSpeed Insights and read the mobile score, not the desktop one. Then throttle your own browser to a slow connection and load the site. It is a sobering exercise and it takes two minutes.

title: Automating the work nobody wants to do
author: Your Name
excerpt: Find the task someone does every week that produces nothing new. That is where automation pays for itself fastest.

content.text: Automation projects go wrong when they start from the technology. They go right when they start from a specific person doing a specific tedious thing on a specific day of the week.
Look for transcription

Any time data moves from one place to another by being retyped, that is a candidate. Form to sheet, sheet to report, report to email. Nothing new is being created — value is only being lost through typos.
Look for the Monday morning ritual
Most businesses have a report someone rebuilds every week, the same way, from the same sources. A scheduled job can build it and email it before anyone arrives.
Count the real cost
Three hours a week is roughly 150 hours a year of someone’s attention, plus the errors that come from doing something repetitive and dull. That is the number to compare the build cost against.
Automate the reliable part first

Start with the steps that follow fixed rules, and leave judgement calls to people. Trying to automate the exceptions first is how automation projects stall — and how they lose the trust of the team using them.

title: Does your website really need an admin panel?
author: Your Name
excerpt: An admin panel adds cost and surface area. Here is how to decide what genuinely needs to be editable.

content.text: Making everything editable sounds like generosity. In practice an admin panel for content that never changes adds build cost, more code to secure, and one more place a site can be broken by accident.
Make editable what actually changes

items: Portfolio and project entries — these grow constantly.

content.text: Leave in code what does not

Page layout, section order, legal text and the design system itself. These change once a year at most, and making them editable usually means giving someone the ability to break the site’s appearance with a stray value.
The middle ground

Site settings — logo, brand name, contact details, hero headline, social URLs — belong in a settings table even on a small site. They are cheap to make editable and awkward to change in code later, especially when the person who needs to change them is not a developer.
